title: Short Stuff: Fruit Flies, Why?
summary: Short Stuff episode on fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster). The hosts cover their use in scientific research: the V2 rocket flight that carried fruit flies to space and their safe return, their role in establishing modern genetics through Thomas Hunt Morgan's chromosome work and multiple Nobel Prize winners, and why they are useful models (fast generations, easy breeding, cheap care, about 8,000 of 20,000 to 25,000 human genes analogous to fruit fly genes, shared biochemical pathways and brain structures relevant to Alzheimer's, and use as models for mosquito disease transmission). They end with the downsides: fruit flies are a cosmopolitan pest attracted to overripe fruit and compost, do not transmit human disease, and can be trapped with a vinegar jar and plastic wrap.

segments.title: Opening banter and naming fruit flies
segments.summary: The hosts joke about confusing fruit flies with tsetse flies and debate how to pronounce Drosophila melanogaster, then settle on calling them fruit flies.

segments.title: Fruit flies in space
segments.summary: Fruit flies were loaded on a V2 rocket that reached about 67 miles up, described as one mile into space by NASA. They were the first animals sent to space and survived the flight and re-entry, which paved the way for larger animals and eventually humans.
topics: V2 rocket fruit fly space flight

segments.title: Fruit flies and the founding of modern genetics
segments.summary: Fruit flies were used in biological studies for more than a decade by the 1930s. Thomas Hunt Morgan used them to show inheritance passes through chromosomes, faster than other early geneticists, and at least five people have won Nobel Prizes working with fruit flies.

segments.title: Why fruit flies are good lab subjects
segments.summary: Fruit flies produce a new generation in about two weeks, are easy and cheap to breed and care for, and eat a cornstarch and sugar mixture. They share about 8,000 of the roughly 20,000 to 25,000 human genes in analogous form, so studies can extrapolate to people, including disease-linked genes and experiments on cold-temperature effects on metabolism.

segments.title: Alzheimer's pathways and other research uses
segments.summary: Fruit flies do not develop Alzheimer's but share the biochemical pathways and brain structures affected by it, so researchers study them to look for treatments.

segments.title: Fruit fly pests and their role as research models
segments.summary: Fruit flies are a cosmopolitan species found wherever humans live, drawn to overripe fruit and compost. They do not transmit communicable diseases, but they have served as models for studying disease-carrying mosquitoes. Trapping them with a vinegar jar covered by plastic wrap with holes is suggested.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with a joke about thanking fruit flies rather than swatting them and end the show.
